questions.q: Per this lesson's four-question framework, what should be decided first when designing any new integration?
options: Who owns this data -- decided per field or domain, before anything else gets designed
Which middleware vendor to use
How many Apex classes the integration will require
Whether to use REST or SOAP
questions.explain: Lesson 1's system-of-record decision comes first in the framework because every other design choice -- sync direction, conflict handling, access -- depends on knowing which system is authorized to originate which data.

questions.q: Which two lesson examples does this wrap-up connect as both being, underneath, answers to the 'what's the blast radius if this integration is slow or down' question asked too late?
options: Lesson 2's CDC design and Lesson 4's sharing sets
Lesson 3's SAML design and Lesson 6's middleware hub discussion
Lesson 5's callout-in-a-trigger failure and Lesson 7's ERP-outage incident
Lesson 1's External ID design and Lesson 8 itself
questions.explain: Both failures trace back to a critical user action being coupled, without enough thought to blast radius, to the availability of an external system -- exactly the question this framework asks architects to raise before building, not after an incident.

questions.q: Why would Doverfield's event-driven, slightly-delayed order-creation pattern (Lesson 1) be the wrong choice for the live shipping-rate lookup (Lesson 5)?
options: Event-driven patterns cannot technically call external shipping APIs
Order creation and shipping rates both require exactly the same freshness requirement, so the pattern should transfer directly
Shipping-rate lookups are not a valid integration use case

The rep needs an answer immediately while sitting at the screen, which an asynchronous, delay-tolerant pattern doesn't provide -- a pattern's fit depends on the specific freshness requirement, not on whether it worked elsewhere
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that pattern fit depends on the specific combination of requirements for that integration -- a pattern that works well for a delay-tolerant case can be the wrong fit for a case where the user needs an immediate answer.

questions.q: What does this lesson say Chapter 2 does differently with the same case-study pairings introduced in Chapter 1?
options: Chapter 2 goes deep on specific mechanics Chapter 1 only had room to introduce -- detailed ownership/conflict design, failure handling, extraction at volume, federation detail, portal scale, and callout resilience
Chapter 2 abandons all of Chapter 1's patterns and starts over with entirely new scenarios
Chapter 2 is purely a repeat of Chapter 1's content with different company names
Chapter 2 focuses exclusively on customer portals and skips every other case study
questions.explain: Chapter 2's six deep-dive lessons revisit several of Chapter 1's case-study pairings at a level of mechanical detail Chapter 1 didn't have room to cover.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why is 'it worked for Doverfield's ERP integration' not, by itself, a justification for reusing that same pattern on a new integration?
options: Because ERP integrations are fundamentally different from every other kind of integration
Because Salesforce prohibits reusing integration patterns across different objects

Because a pattern is a fit for a specific combination of ownership, freshness, blast-radius, and access requirements -- not universally good, so each new case needs the four-question framework re-applied rather than the last answer copied
Because every integration must use a unique pattern never used before in the same org
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns against copying a working pattern without re-asking the four questions for the new integration's own specific requirements.
